kurz: Which decision the option writer hands over in return for the premium, what the business earns and costs, and how the tax office treats it.

bloecke.md:
When an option is sold, no security is handed over; the seller enters into an obligation. The buyer pays for the right to decide over the next few weeks. The [[option writer]] takes the money and gives up the decision. The premium comes in immediately and is received for good, which is what makes the business attractive. In return, the obligation continues until expiry.

For a private portfolio, only two structures are justifiable, because with them the worst case is known in advance. These are the covered call on shares that are already in the portfolio and the cash-secured put, for which the money to take delivery is set aside. The uncovered short call, with its theoretically unlimited loss, is not one of them, no matter how high the premium is.

A Eurex equity option contract is usually for 100 shares. The exchange's contract specification is binding, and after corporate actions the number of shares can differ. All the following figures are illustrative calculations using Black-Scholes, so that premium, delta and probability are consistent with one another. They are not market quotations.

## The covered call

The portfolio holds 100 shares at €100, so the capital tied up is €10,000. A call with a strike price of 105 and 60 days remaining is written on these shares. With 25% implied volatility, a 2.5% interest rate and a 2% dividend yield, the model gives a premium of €2.13 per share, or €213 per contract. The delta of the short position is −0.34, and the modelled probability of expiring in the money is around 30%.

From €105 upwards, the gain is capped. On the downside, almost nothing changes, because the premium only offsets a price fall of €2.13 per share. Below that, the portfolio loses as much as it would without the call. A covered call therefore swaps upside potential for cash and is not a hedge.

bloecke.formel: Result per share = min(S_T, K) − S_0 + P
bloecke.erklaerung: The gain is capped at the strike price K; the loss is not. The break-even point is S_0 − P.
variablen: Strike price of the call sold
bloecke.beispiel: K = 105, S_0 = 100, P = 2.13. At S_T = 118, the result is min(118, 105) − 100 + 2.13 = €7.13 per share. The remaining €13 per share of the price movement goes to the buyer of the call.

bloecke.titel: Covered call with the share at 100 and a short call 105 for 2.13
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation. Above the kink at 105, the result rises no further, and the break-even point is 97.87. The downside buffer equals the amount of the premium.

bloecke.md:
## The cash-secured put

With a cash-secured put, money is held ready instead of shares. A put with a strike price of 95 and likewise 60 days to expiry costs €1.90 per share in the model, or €190 per contract. The amount to be secured is €9,500, because that is what taking delivery of the shares costs if the price falls. The gain is limited to the premium, and the loss to €9,310 in the event that the share falls to zero.

The risk resembles that of buying shares, but the asymmetry is reversed. You never get more than €1.90 per share, but in the extreme case you lose €93.10. This profile corresponds to that of an insurance policy, and the put is priced accordingly.

bloecke.formel: Result per share = P − max(K − S_T, 0)
bloecke.erklaerung: If the price at expiry is above K, the full premium is kept. Below K, the option writer bears every euro of price loss one for one. The break-even point is K − P.
variablen: Strike price of the put sold
bloecke.beispiel: K = 95, P = 1.90. At S_T = 80, the result is 1.90 − 15 = −€13.10 per share. The shares still have to be bought at 95; the effective entry price is 93.10.

bloecke.titel: The two structures compared (illustrative calculation, 60 days)
zeilen: Model probability of expiring in the money

bloecke.md: With the same strike price, the covered call and the cash-secured put are synthetically identical. This follows from put-call parity. In the model, the covered call on 105 brings in a maximum of €7.13 per share, and the short put on 105 brings in €7.03 in premium. The difference of 0.10 corresponds exactly to the balance of the interest on the higher cash collateral (0.43 over 60 days) and the dividend that only the shareholder receives (0.33). It is therefore not an advantage of the covered call. If you consider one of the two variants to be better, you have overlooked interest or dividends.

bloecke.titel: Result per contract after 60 days, depending on the closing price
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation in euros. With an unchanged price and slight pullbacks, option writing does better than the share. Sharp price falls lead to losses; with sharp rises, the result remains positive but is far below that of the share.

bloecke.md:
## Realistic return expectations

A return of 2.13% in 60 days can be extrapolated to around 13% a year. This extrapolation is the most common self-deception in option writing. It assumes that a premium of this size is available six times in a row. However, premiums are only high when volatility is high, and such an environment is rarely calm. In addition, the extrapolation ignores the cycles in which the call is exercised and the shares are gone while the price keeps rising. Finally, it is calculated before tax and before the spread.

The economic reason why anything is left over at all is the volatility risk premium. On a long-term average, implied volatility is above the volatility realised later. Option writers earn money from this, but in the role of an insurer, with many small gains and rare, very large losses. Position size must therefore be based on the maximum loss and not on the premium.

Eleven months with a premium of €200 each come to €2,200. If the position has to be bought back for €1,900 in the twelfth month, €500 is left before tax, including that month's premium. Such months are part of the structure, because the distribution of outcomes is heavy on the left. A success rate of 80% or 90% says nothing about the expected return as long as the average size of the losses is not stated alongside it.

## Allocation, rolling, assignment risk

Eurex equity options can usually be exercised American-style. An assignment can therefore come at any time, not only on the expiry date, and the clearing house allocates it by random draw. In practice, this mainly affects short calls that are in the money. They are often exercised on the day before the ex-dividend date, because the option holder only receives the dividend if they own the share beforehand. As soon as the remaining time value is smaller than the dividend, early exercise is rational for the holder. Option writers who do not allow for this find an empty share portfolio the next morning.

Index options such as ODAX or OESX, on the other hand, are European-style and cash-settled. With them there is no early assignment and no delivery; at expiry, only a cash payment is made.

When **rolling**, the current option is bought back and a new one with a later expiry is sold, often with a different strike price. Executed as a combination order, this costs the spread once instead of twice. In economic terms, however, rolling does not eliminate a loss. Anyone who pushes a deep in-the-money call further out has turned a realised loss into a longer bet and received a small premium for it. Rolling makes sense where the original market expectation still holds. If it has been refuted, it is more consistent to close the position.

## The wheel strategy

The wheel combines both structures into a cycle. The option writer sells a put below the current price, takes over the shares on assignment and writes calls on them above the entry price. When the calls are exercised, the writer is back in cash, and the cycle starts again. The following illustrative calculation shows a year with four quarterly cycles on a share that starts at 100, falls to 88 in between and closes at 104.

bloecke.titel: Wheel year with 100 shares (illustrative calculation, 25% implied volatility)

bloecke.md:
The premiums add up to 268 + 180 + 188 + 241 = €877. The shares were taken over for €9,500 and handed over for €10,000, which brings in +€500. Together that makes €1,377 on around €10,000 of capital that was tied up throughout the year, or 13.8% before tax.

With buy-and-hold, on the other hand, a rise from 100 to 104 would have produced €400 or 4.0%. Dividends are left out of both calculations; buy-and-hold would have received one more quarter of them.

The counter-example is also part of the picture. If the same share had risen from 100 to 130 without any pullback, no put would ever have been assigned. An option writer who moves the strike prices up each time to around 5% below the market then collects just over 10% in premiums over four quarters and misses out on a 30% price gain. The wheel is a short volatility position with capped profit and almost full price risk, and not a reliable source of income.

## Taxes in Germany

Option writing is taxed differently from share transactions, and this is where most return calculations fail. The decisive provision is Section 20(1) no. 11 EStG (Income Tax Act), which makes the premium received a separate type of income:

> Premiums received by option writers for the granting of options; where the option writer enters into a closing transaction, the premiums paid in the closing transaction are to be taken into account as negative income at the time of payment.

Three consequences follow from this. First, the premium is taxable at the moment it is received, regardless of how the transaction turns out. Second, the premium paid on the buy-back reduces the income. According to the tax authorities, this also applies to the incidental costs of the buy-back and to the order fees on selling the option (BMF circular of 14 May 2025, paras. 25 and 33). Other costs fall under the ban on deducting income-related expenses (Werbungskostenabzugsverbot) in Section 20(9) EStG, which allows no deduction of costs beyond the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000. Third, since the Annual Tax Act 2024 (Jahressteuergesetz), the time of payment is what counts. Previously, the buy-back was related back to the year in which the premium was received, which the Federal Fiscal Court (BFH) had treated as a retroactive event.

bloecke.titel: Four possible outcomes and their tax treatment
zeilen: The premium is kept in full
Income under Section 20(1) no. 11 EStG, already taxed on receipt
Negative income at the time of payment, Section 20(1) no. 11 EStG
The option writer pays the difference
Not a closing transaction; according to the prevailing view, a loss from a derivative transaction (Termingeschäft), Section 20(2) sentence 1 no. 3 EStG
Shares are delivered or taken over
The share transaction is recorded separately under Section 20(2) sentence 1 no. 1 EStG; the premium remains income under no. 11 and is not included in the acquisition costs

bloecke.md:
The separation of the loss pots matters in practice. Under Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG, losses from share sales may only be offset against gains from share sales, while premiums and derivative transactions go into the general loss pot (allgemeiner Verlusttopf). The former limit of €20,000 on offsetting losses from derivative transactions has no longer been in the law since the Annual Tax Act 2024. Older guides that still mention it are out of date on this point. It remains the case that losses from capital assets cannot be offset against employment income or rental income. They can only be carried forward.

The usual tax rate of 25% capital income withholding tax (Kapitalertragsteuer) plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge applies, together 26.375%. For those liable to church tax, it is around 27.8% to 28.0%. Domestic institutions withhold the tax directly. However, most German direct banks do not offer the writing of Eurex options at all. Investors who write options through a foreign broker have no tax withheld at source and must declare everything themselves in the capital income annex (Anlage KAP). This does not create a tax advantage. The payment is merely deferred, which has an interest effect, and an obligation to file a return is added.

bloecke.titel: Closing out after the turn of the year
bloecke.md: An option is sold in December for €2,000 and bought back in January for €2,600. In economic terms, that is a loss of €600. For tax purposes, €2,000 of income has to be taxed in the first year, which results in €527.50 of tax. The €2,600 only takes effect as negative income in the second year. An option writer who has only collected premiums in December and carries the open positions over into the new year therefore pays tax on a result that has not yet been determined.

- Only write options on securities that you wanted to hold or buy anyway. The strike price is the price to which you commit yourself contractually.
- Base the position size on the maximum loss and not on the premium. A short put on 95 is an obligation of €9,500.
- Before every ex-dividend date, check whether a short call is in the money and how much time value is left.
- Use combination orders for rolling and not two separate orders.
- Before the turn of the year, make a deliberate decision about open short positions instead of letting them run.
- As a comparison, always calculate the simple alternative as well, that is, holding the share or investing the money at interest.

bloecke.titel: The popularity of the covered call
bloecke.md:
Many investors experience the covered call like rental income from a security. Money comes in regularly, the hit rate is high, and the success is visible on the account statement. This feedback is misleading, because the structure delivers many small confirmations and the rare big disappointment only comes later.

In addition, there is a counting error. The upward movement that was sold does not appear on any statement. If an investor has to hand over the shares at 105 and the price then rises to 130, the investor has lost €2,500 per contract, which does not show up as a loss on any securities account statement. A complete record therefore contains an additional column with the price of the underlying on the expiry date.

mitnehmen: The premium is the payment for the option buyer's right to decide, and so it is not income without anything in return.
A covered call and a cash-secured put with the same strike price are the same transaction; the difference in the result is fully explained by interest and dividends.
The gain is capped, while almost all of the price risk remains, because a premium of 2% only offsets a fall of 2%.
The premium is taxable immediately on receipt, while the buy-back only takes effect on payment, so that over the turn of the year tax can become due on a result that does not yet exist.
The wheel is a short volatility position with full price risk and capped profit, and not a reliable source of income.

begriffe.text: Seller of an option. The writer collects the premium and takes on the obligation to deliver (call) or take delivery of (put) the underlying at the strike price.
Sale of a call on shares already held in the portfolio. The result per share is min(S_T, K) − S_0 + premium. The gain is capped; the price risk remains almost unchanged.
Sale of a put for which the purchase price for a possible assignment is deposited in cash. The maximum profit is the premium; the maximum loss is the strike price minus the premium.
Allocation following exercise by the option holder. For American-style equity options, it can happen at any time during the term and is assigned by random draw by the clearing house.
Buying back an option that has been sold, before expiry. Under Section 20(1) no. 11 EStG (Income Tax Act), the premium paid is to be taken into account as negative income at the time of payment.
Cycle of cash-secured put, assignment, covered call and renewed sale. Economically, it is a short volatility position with capped profit and full price risk.
